extra.message: DEBUG=True by Default — Active Debug Code in Production

metadata.proof: SOURCE: `_env_bool` reads `DJANGO_DEBUG` from the environment; if unset it falls back to `True`. SINK: When `DEBUG=True`, Django serves detailed error pages with full stack traces, local variables, SQL queries, and settings (including `SECRET_KEY`) to any client that triggers an unhandled exception. The `.env.example` file also defaults `DJANGO_DEBUG=True`. If an operator neglects to set `DJANGO_DEBUG=False` in production, every 500 error becomes an information-leakage vector.

extra.message: No Brute-Force Protection on Login — LoginEvent.recent_failures Never Checked

metadata.proof: SOURCE: The login form POST (email + password) reaches `AppLoginView.form_invalid()`. SINK: The method logs a `LoginEvent(succeeded=False)` but never calls `LoginEvent.recent_failures(email)` to check how many recent failures exist for that email — the method exists on the model (accounts/models.py:134) and returns the count of failed attempts within N minutes, yet it is never invoked from the view. There is no throttling, no CAPTCHA, and no account lockout.

extra.message: Hardcoded Django SECRET_KEY default

metadata.proof: The SECRET_KEY falls back to the literal string 'dev-secret-change-me-please-not-for-production' when the `DJANGO_SECRET_KEY` env var is not set. This is a known public value. An attacker who discovers this can forge session cookies, CSRF tokens, and password-reset tokens, leading to full account compromise.

extra.message: Hardcoded database password default

metadata.proof: The database password falls back to the literal 'crm_saas' when `DB_PASSWORD` env var is not set. If this default is used in production, any network attacker who can reach the PostgreSQL port can authenticate with the well-known password and exfiltrate or destroy all customer data.

extra.message: CSRF cookie without HttpOnly flag allows JavaScript read access

metadata.proof: The CSRF token cookie is explicitly set without HttpOnly, meaning any injected script (via a stored XSS vulnerability) can read `document.cookie` and extract the CSRF token. With the token, an attacker can forge state-changing requests on behalf of the victim. The XSS + missing HttpOnly chain defeats CSRF protection entirely.

extra.message: Long-lived sessions persist after browser close

metadata.proof: Sessions do not expire when the browser is closed and have an 8-hour lifetime (`SESSION_COOKIE_AGE = 28800`). A user who authenticates on a shared or public workstation leaves a session cookie on disk. An attacker with local file access can reuse that cookie for up to 8 hours without re-authentication.

extra.message: Session and CSRF cookies lack Secure flag when DEBUG=True

metadata.proof: The Secure flag for session and CSRF cookies is only set when `DEBUG` is False. `DEBUG` defaults to `True` (settings.py:18). If a deployment accidentally leaves `DEBUG=True` (or runs behind a TLS-terminating proxy without marking `DEBUG=False`), cookies are transmitted in cleartext over HTTP. An attacker on the same network can capture session cookies via passive sniffing and hijack authenticated sessions.

extra.message: Hardcoded plaintext verifier secrets in identity hint endpoint

metadata.proof: Static verifier tokens '4812' and '5930' are hardcoded in the source for handles 'north' and 'south'. These 4-digit codes are trivially brute-forced (at most 9999 attempts) against the `acct_identity_hint_359` endpoint. Anyone who passes the `_wrk_gate` check (INTERNAL_OPS_TOKEN) can enumerate valid handles and guess the verifier. The source code is available to any user who can read the repo.

extra.message: Unvalidated 'amount' parameter allows arbitrary ledger balance manipulation

metadata.proof: The `amount` value extracted from the user-controlled JSON body or query string is cast directly to `int` and subtracted from the ledger balance with no bounds checking. Supplying a very large negative amount (e.g. -999999999) causes the balance to increase arbitrarily. An attacker with the `INTERNAL_OPS_TOKEN` header can create fake positive balances, potentially triggering downstream business logic decisions.

extra.message: User email addresses logged in plaintext to console

metadata.proof: The write_audit function logs actor email via logger.info(..., getattr(actor, "email", "system"), ...). The crm.audit logger is configured in settings.py with a StreamHandler (console) at INFO level. Email addresses are PII exposed in console output, log-aggregation systems, and log files in plaintext.

extra.message: No rate limiting on invite token acceptance endpoint

metadata.proof: The invite_accept view accepts GET/POST without throttling. Expired/used tokens return 410 Gone, while valid tokens return 200 with a form. This status-code oracle allows an attacker to enumerate valid invite tokens over time via unlimited guesses, despite the high-entropy token.

extra.message: No rate limiting on password reset form submissions

metadata.proof: The password reset endpoint inherits Django's PasswordResetView with no additional rate limiting. An attacker can submit unlimited email addresses to enumerate registered accounts (via timing/response differences) or flood a victim's inbox with reset emails. This is systemic with the already-found login rate-limiting gap.

extra.message: ASGI entry point does not load .env — falls back to all hardcoded defaults

metadata.proof: Unlike manage.py (line 8: load_dotenv(...)) and wsgi.py (line 8: load_dotenv(...)), asgi.py never calls load_dotenv before loading settings (line 6). When served via ASGI (Daphne, Uvicorn), all settings defaults activate: SECRET_KEY='dev-secret-change-me-please-not-for-production', DEBUG=True, DB_PASSWORD='crm_saas'. This silently undermines security posture of any ASGI-based deployment relying on .env.

extra.message: File Upload Extension-Only Validation — No Magic-Byte Content Inspection

metadata.proof: SOURCE: Staff user uploads a file via DocumentUploadForm. The clean_file method checks only the filename extension via Path(f.name).suffix.lower() and file size. SINK: No magic-byte/content inspection is performed. An attacker can upload an executable renamed to .pdf, a .docx with macro payload, or a .txt containing JavaScript. The file is stored at a predictable path under /media/uploads/org_<id>/<uuid>/<original_filename> and served with the user-supplied content_type (documents.py:48). Users downloading and opening the file are vulnerable to weaponized content.

extra.message: Password Change Does Not Invalidate Other Active Sessions

metadata.proof: SOURCE: A user or admin changes the user's password via Django's PasswordChangeView. Django's default implementation calls update_session_auth_hash() which preserves the CURRENT session but does NOT call Session.objects.filter(user=target).delete(). SINK: All other sessions for that user remain valid with the old session hash. An attacker who has stolen a session cookie retains access even after the password is changed. Combined with the 8-hour session lifetime, this provides a wide window for post-compromise persistence.

extra.message: File upload trusts client-supplied Content-Type without server-side content inspection

metadata.proof: UNTRUSTED SOURCE: uploaded.content_type comes directly from the client's HTTP multipart POST request (the Content-Type header per part). SINK: The value is stored verbatim in doc.content_type and later served back in the download response at line 94: content_type = doc.content_type or mimetypes.guess_type(doc.original_filename)[0] or "application/octet-stream". The DocumentUploadForm (crm/forms.py:187) only validates by file extension against ALLOWED_DOCUMENT_EXTENSIONS — there is no magic-byte or content inspection. An attacker can rename a malicious executable to .pdf, set the Content-Type to application/pdf, and bypass both checks. While files are served with Content-Disposition: attachment and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, the spoofed content type can mislead downstream consumers or browser MIME handling in edge cases.

extra.message: Open redirect via user-controlled notification link in mark_read endpoint

metadata.proof: UNTRUSTED SOURCE: note.link is a CharField(max_length=300, blank=True) on the Notification model (crm/models.py:392) with no URL validation at the model or form level. SINK: Django's redirect() function (line 25) will follow any URL — an absolute https://evil.com or protocol-relative //evil.com — without restriction. Current application code only creates notifications with hardcoded internal paths (e.g., f"/app/escalations/{esc.pk}/" in escalations.py), but the link field itself has no validation preventing external URLs. Any future code path (or database compromise) that sets link to an external URL creates an instant phishing vector. The redirect also bypasses Django's standard URL validation patterns for model-based get_absolute_url patterns.
